injection.title: The Sorcerer's Apprentice
injection.story: While the sorcerer was away, his apprentice enchanted a broom to carry water. The apprentice knew how to start the work, but not how to stop it. Soon the basin overflowed. Determined to fix the problem himself, he split the broom with an axe. Both pieces rose and carried more water, making the flood worse. When the sorcerer returned, he stopped the spell. The apprentice looked at the flooded room and understood that making something happen was different from knowing when and how it should happen.
injection.facts: Scenario outline: a sorcerer is absent. An apprentice can enchant a broom to carry water but does not know the stopping spell. The broom continues after the basin is full, causing an overflow. The apprentice's attempted repair is to split the broom with an axe. Both pieces then carry water, increasing the flood. The returning sorcerer stops the spell. The flooded room illustrates the distinction between being able to initiate an action and understanding when that action is appropriate and how it can be stopped.

label.title: The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs
label.story: A farmer owned a goose that laid one golden egg each morning. The daily gift brought steady prosperity, but the farmer grew impatient. One egg seemed too little when there must surely be a store of gold inside the bird. Hoping to collect the whole treasure at once, the farmer killed the goose and opened it. There was no hidden treasure. The farmer had exchanged a lasting source of value for a hurried attempt to show a larger gain, and now there would be no more golden eggs.
label.facts: Scenario outline: a farmer owns a goose producing one golden egg each morning. The eggs provide steady prosperity. Dissatisfaction with the rate of return leads the farmer to assume, without evidence, that a larger store of gold is inside the bird. The farmer kills and opens the goose in an attempt to obtain that store immediately. No hidden treasure exists. The intervention destroys the source of future golden eggs. The immediate attempt at a larger visible gain therefore eliminates a continuing source of value rather than improving it.
